entities.summary:
Algeria, officially the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, is the largest country in Africa (2,381,741 km²) and tenth largest in the world, located in the Maghreb region of North Africa. It is bordered by Tunisia and Libya to the northeast, Niger and Mali to the south, Mauritania and Western Sahara to the southwest, and Morocco to the west. The vast Sahara Desert covers over 80% of Algeria's territory, concentrating most of its 46 million people in the fertile Mediterranean coastal strip.

Algeria's history spans over 8,000 years of continuous habitation. Berber (Amazigh) civilization dominated the region through classical antiquity, with the Numidian kingdom (3rd–1st centuries BCE) allying with Rome against Carthage. Roman Algeria (Numidia province) became one of the most prosperous regions of the empire — birthplace of Saint Augustine (354–430 CE). The Arab conquest (670s CE) spread Islam through the Maghreb. Ottoman Algeria (1516–1830) became the most powerful Barbary state in the Mediterranean. French Algeria (1830–1962) was the defining colonial experience — a settler colony of 1.2 million Europeans alongside 9 million Muslim Algerians — that produced the brutal War of Independence (1954–1962) costing over a million lives.

Independence in 1962 under FLN leadership established a one-party Arab socialist state. Algeria became a major oil and gas exporter (joining OPEC 1969), with hydrocarbons accounting for 95% of export revenues. The Civil War (1991–2002), triggered by the military's cancellation of elections won by Islamists, killed 100,000–200,000 Algerians and remains the defining trauma of the post-independence generation.
